title: Can I claim R&D credits for internal-use software?
description: Internal-use software qualifies for the federal R&D credit only if it passes the four general tests and the three-part high threshold of innovation test.
summary: U.S. businesses that develop internal-use software (IUS) for general and administrative functions can claim the federal R&D tax credit only if the project passes the four general qualified research tests and a three-part high threshold of innovation test under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6), backed by records strong enough to survive an IRS examination.

body.text: U.S. businesses that develop internal-use software (IUS) for general and administrative functions can claim the federal R&D tax credit only if the project passes the four general qualified research tests and a three-part high threshold of innovation test under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6), backed by records strong enough to survive an IRS examination.

This report is general information for U.S. federal income tax purposes, not tax or legal advice. Readers should confirm the application of these rules to their own facts with a qualified tax advisor.
Short answer

Yes, but only if the project clears a higher bar than other software research. Software developed primarily for internal use is excluded from the federal research credit by statute, except to the extent the Treasury regulations allow it. Under the final regulations (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)), internal-use software (IUS) qualifies only if it meets the general requirements for qualified research in IRC § 41(d)(1), is not otherwise excluded under § 41(d)(4), and also passes a three-part "high threshold of innovation" test in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii). In practice that means seven tests in total (four general tests plus three IUS-specific tests), and the claim has to be supported by records strong enough to survive an IRS examination.

Two developments since the IUS regulations were finalized in 2016 now shape every IUS claim. First, the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act (Public Law 119-21) restored current deduction of domestic research and experimental (R&E) expenditures through new IRC § 174A for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, which changes how the credit interacts with cost recovery. Second, Section G of Form 6765 (Business Component Information) is mandatory for most filers for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025, and it requires the taxpayer to state, business component by business component, whether software is internal use software, dual function software, non-internal use software, or excepted from internal use treatment. A taxpayer claiming IUS credits for a 2026 tax year must therefore classify each software component on the face of the return.
The research credit and the cost-recovery rules around it

The credit for increasing research activities is codified in IRC § 41. The statute excludes research on computer software "developed by (or for the benefit of) the taxpayer primarily for internal use by the taxpayer," unless the software is used in an activity that is itself qualified research or in a qualifying production process, and only "to the extent provided in regulations" (§ 41(d)(4)(E)). Congress therefore did not ban IUS from the credit outright; it delegated to Treasury the task of defining when IUS research qualifies, and Treasury exercised that authority in the 2016 final regulations discussed below.

The One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act (Public Law 119-21), enacted July 4, 2025, added IRC § 174A, which allows domestic R&E expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024 to be deducted currently, or, by election under § 174A(c), capitalized and amortized over a period of not less than 60 months. Section 174, as amended, now applies only to foreign R&E expenditures, which continue to be amortized over 15 years beginning with the midpoint of the taxable year in which they are paid or incurred. The IRS issued procedural guidance for these changes in Rev. Proc. 2025-28, released August 28, 2025.
Rev. Proc. 2025-28 provides two routes for domestic R&E expenditures that were capitalized under the prior § 174 rules in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021 and before January 1, 2025:

items: Small business retroactive election. An eligible small business taxpayer (a taxpayer that is not a tax shelter and meets the § 448(c) gross receipts test, with average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less for the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024) could elect to apply § 174A retroactively to domestic R&E expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, generally by amending the affected returns. Rev. Proc. 2025-28 also allowed eligible small businesses to make a late § 280C(c)(2) reduced-credit election, or to revoke a prior one, for those years. Practitioner commentary describes the outside date for these amended-return elections as July 6, 2026; taxpayers that did not act by then should confirm with an advisor whether any route remains open for them.

Recovery of unamortized amounts. Any taxpayer, including one that does not qualify as a small business, may elect to deduct the remaining unamortized balance of domestic R&E expenditures capitalized in 2022 through 2024 either entirely in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, or ratably over the first two taxable years beginning after that date.

body.text: The restoration of current deduction also restored the need to coordinate the credit with the deduction. For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, IRC § 280C(c), as amended, generally requires the taxpayer to reduce its domestic R&E expenditures otherwise taken into account under § 174A by the amount of the research credit, unless the taxpayer elects under § 280C(c)(2) to claim a reduced credit instead. The election must be made on a timely filed original return. For an IUS claim, this means the credit computation and the § 174A deduction should be prepared together rather than separately.

The size of any IUS benefit depends on the taxpayer's qualified research expenses, its base amount, the computation method chosen (regular credit or alternative simplified credit), and the § 280C(c) coordination described above, so no general figure can be stated reliably.
The four general tests every claim must pass

IUS has to satisfy the same four requirements that apply to all qualified research before the IUS-specific tests come into play. These requirements are applied separately to each business component (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)), and if a component as a whole fails, the "shrinking-back" rule applies the tests to successively smaller subsets of that component.
Permitted purpose

The research must relate to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of a business component. Research related to "style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors" never has a qualified purpose (§ 41(d)(3)(B)). The regulation places the qualified-purpose rule within its definition of a process of experimentation, at Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), which states that research is conducted for a qualified purpose if it relates to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component.
Elimination of uncertainty

Research must be intended to discover information that eliminates uncertainty about the development or improvement of a business component. Uncertainty exists when the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the component, or its appropriate design (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3), "Undertaken for the purpose of discovering information"). Uncertainty is judged from the information available to the taxpayer at the beginning of the work, not from hindsight.

That case is Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201, where the Tax Court held that the uncertainty requirement is met when the taxpayer knows a result is technically achievable but is unsure of the method or appropriate design needed to reach it. For IUS, this general-test uncertainty is only the starting point: as discussed below, the significant economic risk prong of the high threshold of innovation test demands a higher level of uncertainty.
Technological in nature

The process used to resolve the uncertainty must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(i); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4); IRS Audit Techniques Guide). The regulation sets out the "technological in nature" definition in paragraph (a)(4); paragraph (a)(5) covers the process of experimentation and the qualified-purpose rule. For software development, computer science is the usual discipline relied on, but the record should show that the developers actually applied those principles to resolve the uncertainty, rather than simply writing code.
Process of experimentation

Substantially all of the research activities must be elements of a process of experimentation (§ 41(d)(1)(C)). The regulation sets "substantially all" at 80 percent or more of the research activities, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, and applied separately to each business component (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6)). A process of experimentation is a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i)). It typically involves identifying the uncertainty, identifying one or more alternatives intended to eliminate it, and conducting a process of evaluating those alternatives through modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error.

The regulation says "one or more alternatives." The underlying point is nevertheless consistent with the regulation, which requires an evaluative process, and with recent Tax Court decisions such as Phoenix Design Group, discussed below.
Is the software internal-use software?

Before the higher threshold applies, the software has to be IUS in the first place. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii), software is developed by (or for the benefit of) the taxpayer primarily for the taxpayer's internal use if it is developed for use in general and administrative functions that facilitate or support the conduct of the taxpayer's trade or business. The regulation limits those general and administrative (G&A) functions to three categories: financial management functions, human resources management functions, and support services functions (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)). The Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) restate the same definition. The table below uses the regulation's own lists, which are introduced with the phrase "include, but are not limited to."

cells: Accounts payable, accounts receivable, inventory management, budgeting, cash management, cost accounting, disbursements, economic analysis and forecasting, financial reporting, finance, fixed asset accounting, general ledger bookkeeping, internal audit, management accounting, risk management, strategic business planning, and tax
Recruiting, hiring, training, assigning personnel, maintaining personnel records, payroll, and benefits

Data processing, facility services (for example grounds keeping, housekeeping, janitorial, and logistics), graphic services, marketing, legal services, government compliance services, printing and publication services, and security services

body.text: Because the regulation's lists are non-exhaustive, software for a function not named in the table (for example, procurement) may still be G&A software if it facilitates or supports the conduct of the business in the same way as the listed functions.
The regulation lists inventory management as a financial management function.
Software that is not IUS, and software exempt from the higher threshold

Software is not developed primarily for internal use if it is developed to be commercially sold, leased, licensed, or otherwise marketed to third parties, or to enable the taxpayer to interact with third parties or allow third parties to initiate functions or review data on the taxpayer's system (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iv)). Software that falls within these categories is tested only under the four general tests, without the high threshold of innovation test.

Separately, the high threshold of innovation test does not apply to three kinds of software even if they are developed for internal use: software used in an activity that constitutes qualified research (other than the development of the internal-use software itself), software used in a production process to which the research requirements are met, and a new or improved package of software and hardware developed together by the taxpayer as a single product, of which the software is an integral part, that is used directly by the taxpayer in providing services in its trade or business (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(ii)). On Form 6765, Section G, such software is reported as "excepted from internal use treatment."

Whether software is IUS depends on the intent of the taxpayer and the facts and circumstances at the beginning of the software development (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(v)). If a taxpayer originally develops software primarily for internal use but later makes improvements to that software with the intent to hold the improved software for sale or other third-party purposes, the improvements are evaluated separately under the same principles. A change in intent after development begins does not retroactively convert the original work.
Dual function software

Software developed both for G&A use and for third-party interaction is dual function software, and it is presumed to be developed primarily for internal use (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(A)). If the taxpayer can identify a subset of elements that only enables third-party interaction, the presumption does not apply to that third-party subset (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(B)). For the remaining dual function software or subset, a safe harbor lets the taxpayer include 25 percent of its qualified research expenditures in computing the credit, if use by third parties (or by the taxpayer to interact with third parties) is reasonably anticipated to constitute at least 10 percent of the software's use, measured by an objective, reasonable method within the taxpayer's industry (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)(C)). The safe harbor is an alternative to proving that the remaining dual function software passes the high threshold of innovation test; a taxpayer that can pass the full test is not limited to 25 percent.

Worked example (hypothetical). A company develops a portal used by its finance staff and by vendors. It identifies no separate third-party subset. It has $400,000 of qualified research expenditures on the portal and, using an objective method such as processing time or number of transactions, reasonably anticipates that vendor use will be 15 percent of total use. Because 15 percent is at least 10 percent, the safe harbor is available: 25% × $400,000 = $100,000 of qualified research expenditures can be included in the credit computation. If anticipated third-party use were 8 percent, the safe harbor would not be available, and the company would have to show that the portal passes the high threshold of innovation test to claim any of its expenditures. On a 2026 Form 6765, the portal would be reported in Section G as dual function software.
The high threshold of innovation test

IUS that passes the four general tests must also pass all three parts of the high threshold of innovation test in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii). The regulation places the burden on the taxpayer: the software qualifies only if "the taxpayer can establish" each element. (The regulation also requires that the research not be otherwise excluded under § 41(d)(4), for example as research after commercial production, adaptation, duplication, or funded research.)
Innovative

The software is innovative if it would result in a reduction in cost or improvement in speed or other measurable improvement that is substantial and economically significant, if the development is or would have been successful. The regulation calls this a measurable objective standard, not a determination of the unique or novel nature of the software or the software development process. Because the test asks what the software would achieve if successful, a project that ultimately fails can still satisfy it.
Significant economic risk

The taxpayer must commit substantial resources to the development, and there must be substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that those resources would be recovered within a reasonable period. The regulation states that this "substantial uncertainty" requires a higher level of uncertainty and technical risk than the general uncertainty test in § 1.41-4(a)(3). It does not require uncertainty about whether the final result can ever be achieved; the question is whether it can be achieved in time for the resources to be recovered. The technical risk must arise from uncertainty that is technological in nature.

Treasury and the IRS stated that IUS research activities involving only uncertainty about appropriate design, and not about capability or methodology, would rarely qualify as having substantial uncertainty for purposes of this prong. A taxpayer whose IUS project involved only design choices among known methods should therefore expect this prong to be difficult to meet, and the technical record should identify any capability or methodology uncertainty specifically.
Not commercially available

The software must not be commercially available for use by the taxpayer, meaning it cannot be purchased, leased, or licensed and used for the intended purpose without modifications that would themselves satisfy the innovative and significant economic risk requirements.

Analysis: First, meeting the innovative and economic risk tests ties the technical record to financial evidence, so cost or speed projections and the resources committed should be documented alongside the engineering work. Second, projects that mainly configure or integrate off-the-shelf software will usually fail the third test unless the modifications themselves meet the first two. Both follow from the regulation text, but they are interpretations, not additional legal requirements.

cells: New or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality; not style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design
Uncertainty about capability, method, or appropriate design
Reliance on physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science
80% or more of activities evaluate one or more alternatives
Substantial, economically significant measurable improvement if successful
Substantial resources and substantial technical uncertainty about recovering them in a reasonable period; design-only uncertainty rarely suffices
Cannot be bought, leased, or licensed and used without qualifying modifications

body.text: When these rules apply

The IUS rules were finalized in T.D. 9786, published in the Federal Register on October 4, 2016 (81 FR 68299). Paragraph (c)(6) applies to taxable years beginning on or after October 4, 2016. For a taxable year that both ends on or after January 20, 2015 and begins before October 4, 2016, the IRS will not challenge return positions consistent with the final paragraph (c)(6) or with the version proposed in 2015 (IRB 2015-5). For taxable years ending before January 20, 2015, taxpayers may follow either the version of § 1.41-4(c)(6) in the April 1, 2003 edition of the Code of Federal Regulations (with the guidance in IRB 2001-5) or the version published in IRB 2002-4 (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(e)). In practice, open years for nearly all taxpayers now fall under the final 2016 rules.
Substantiation and audit exposure
Form 6765, Section G: business component reporting for IUS

Under the Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025), finalized in early 2026, Section G (Business Component Information) is optional for tax years beginning before 2026 and required for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025, subject to limited exceptions (including qualified small businesses electing the payroll tax credit and certain taxpayers below a gross receipts threshold determined under § 448(c)). Section G requires information for each business component, including the type of component and its qualified research expenses broken down by wages, supplies, and contract research. Where the business component is software, the filer must report the software type: internal use software, dual function software, non-internal use software, or excepted from internal use treatment. The IRS had announced in October 2025 that Section G would remain optional for tax year 2025.

For an IUS claim, the Section G requirement means the classification analysis described earlier in this report (G&A function, third-party interaction, dual function presumption, and the (c)(6)(ii) exceptions) is no longer only a matter for workpapers. It is a representation made on the return for each software component, and an examiner can compare it directly with the technical and financial records supporting the claim.
Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner

T.C. Memo. 2024-113, Docket No. 4759-22, filed December 23, 2024. The taxpayer was a multidisciplinary engineering consulting firm focused on mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection systems for buildings, and the projects concerned building systems design, not software. The parties agreed to have the court evaluate three trial projects. The court held that none of them involved qualified research. It judged uncertainty objectively, based on the information available to the taxpayer, and found that uncertainty in one subcomponent did not make an entire system uncertain when the taxpayer did not connect the two. It found the testimony largely conclusory, the design drawings unexplained, and the hour records not organized in a way that tied time to the claimed uncertainties; it was also skeptical that employees had followed the taxpayer's described design process, based on the narratives in the hours sheets. Following the parties' stipulation, the taxpayer was liable for accuracy-related penalties for each year with a deficiency.
Suder v. Commissioner

T.C. Memo. 2014-201, filed October 1, 2014. The company developed telephone systems and software; the case was not decided under the IUS rules. The court found that 11 of 12 sample projects were qualified research; the one that failed changed only colors, fonts, and button shapes, a cosmetic purpose. The IRS challenged the CEO's wages, which made up roughly two-thirds of wage QREs. The court held those wages unreasonable under § 174(e) and allowed a reduced, reasonable amount. It accepted the company's percentage-of-time allocations as reasonable estimates, and it did not impose accuracy-related penalties.

Analysis: for an IUS claim, these cases point to keeping records made at the time the work is done that identify the specific technical uncertainty, the alternatives evaluated, and the time and cost tied to each, and to having a documented basis for the time allocated to senior personnel. For IUS specifically, the record should also contain the financial evidence that the innovative and significant economic risk prongs require, and evidence that commercially available software was considered and found inadequate without qualifying modifications. With Section G now mandatory, those records should be organized by the same business components reported on Form 6765.
Cost of a disallowed claim

If a credit is disallowed, the resulting underpayment bears interest from the original due date until paid (IRC § 6601(a)), and an accuracy-related penalty of 20 percent of the underpayment can apply, including for negligence or disregard of rules or regulations (IRC § 6662(a), (b)(1)).

Analysis: whatever provider prepares the claim, the regulations call for the same evidence: a technical record showing each of the seven tests, financial support for the innovative and economic risk tests, and cost allocations that can be traced to specific business components. A multidisciplinary review is one way to assemble that record; the law does not prescribe a particular review process. From tax years beginning in 2026, that record must also support the software-type classification reported for each component in Section G of Form 6765.
Conclusion

Internal-use software can qualify for the federal research credit. Software developed for financial management, human resources, or support service functions must pass the four general tests and the three-part high threshold of innovation test in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6), and dual function software may use the 25 percent safe harbor when third-party use is reasonably anticipated to reach 10 percent. Recent Tax Court cases show that claims are lost when the records do not tie specific technical uncertainties and experimentation to the time and costs claimed. Any current claim should also reflect the 2025 changes that moved domestic R&E cost recovery to § 174A and revived the § 280C(c) coordination between the deduction and the credit, and, for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025, the mandatory Section G reporting on Form 6765, which requires each software business component to be classified as internal use, dual function, non-internal use, or excepted.
